title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning andForgetting in On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model
post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting
remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR),
and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources.
It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention,
and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes
retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the
target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of
SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss.
Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution
change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than
in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes,
we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the
student’s pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the
task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make
student updates more concentrated in-domain.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Post-training enables language models to acquire new skills, but can erode capabilities learned during pretraining ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Compared with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on fixed, off-policy responses, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often preserves prior capabilities better, a behavior linked to on-policy data and limited distributional change ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated responses with token-level teacher supervision ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . OPD shares the on-policy setting, yet retention outcomes vary substantially across teacher configurations ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . This raises the question of how OPD compares with SFT and RLVR in learning and capability retention, and how teacher choice shapes these outcomes. To answer the above question, we introduce OPDArena, a framework that systematically compares SFT, RLVR, and OPD across five Base models and four types of OPD teachers under a shared mathematical post-training setup. Figure 1 summarizes this comparison and reveals distinct learning and retention patterns: 1) RLVR and Self-OPD (RLVR) combine mathematical gains with strong retention, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) stays close to Base accuracy in both domains. 2) OPD from larger teachers and Self-OPD (SFT) incur more severe forgetting, while SFT has the largest average capability loss. To understand these differences, we examine changes in predictive distributions. Across methods, OOD change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. This motivates examining update selectivity, measured by OOD prediction change per unit of in-domain change, in relation to the information teachers provide relative to student Base. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that the preferences they acquire through SFT or RLVR concentrate student updates more strongly in-domain. The student’s own distribution further shapes how these preferences contribute to updates, helping explain the different rates at which task gains and forgetting are inherited. Our contributions are: • A systematic evaluation framework. OPDArena compares SFT, RLVR, and OPD teacher sources under a shared setup, jointly characterizing target-domain learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. • A refined view of distribution change and retention. We show that OOD distribution change is more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain change across student models and teacher configurations. We further use the OOD-to-in-domain change ratio, ρ \rho , to characterize update selectivity. • Teacher information and update selectivity. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that preferences acquired through SFT or RLVR improve student update selectivity. Further analyses identify mismatches between teacher-preferred responses and the student’s distribution that can hinder task learning, helping explain why task gains and forgetting transfer at different rates. (b) In-domain accuracy gain versus OOD accuracy gain from Base; colors identify methods and shapes identify models. Ellipses summarize variation across model–teacher configurations. RLVR and Self-OPD (RLVR) combine task learning with low forgetting.

sections.heading: 2  Method
sections.text: We compare post-training methods applied to the same released Qwen Base models and measure their effects on mathematical learning and general capability retention. Our framework distinguishes how supervision enters the model from how its predictions change across domains. We first describe the training signals and teacher configurations (Section 2.1 ), then define how we measure learning, forgetting, and distribution change (Section 2.2 ).

sections.heading: Training feedback.
sections.text: Our RLVR baseline uses group relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) with verifiable correctness rewards. Centering and scaling rewards within each group of responses to the same problem gives a relative advantage shared by all tokens in a response. OPD assigns token-dependent advantages through the teacher–student log-probability ratio. We use a student-weighted Top-16 approximation ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Input formats and the actor update settings are given in Appendices B.2 and B.4 .

sections.heading: Teacher source.
sections.text: We study self-distillation from post-trained checkpoints, distinguishing Self-OPD (SFT) and Self-OPD (RLVR) by how the teacher is trained. We reuse the final saved checkpoints of the corresponding SFT and RLVR experiments reported here as frozen teachers. Each student starts from the same released Base model used in its teacher’s training. OPD from larger models uses frozen Base teachers with more parameters than the student, drawn from the same or a different model family. We use OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) as a representative of self-distillation with privileged information, where the teacher receives additional context unavailable to the student. Within our shared OPD recipe, a frozen copy of the student’s Base model receives the problem and a reference solution, while the student receives only the problem and learns from the teacher’s probabilities on student-generated prefixes.

sections.heading: Models and methods.
sections.text: We experiment with the Qwen2.5 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) (1.5B and 7B) and Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) (1.7B, 4B, and 8B) model families. We use their pretrained Base versions to compare post-training methods and teacher sources from a shared starting point before instruction tuning. For each model, all methods start from the same Base checkpoint. We compare the SFT, RLVR, and OPD configurations defined in Section 2.1 . As shown in Figure 1 (a), Self-OPD uses an SFT or RLVR endpoint as the frozen teacher for a new student initialized from Base.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We train the five Base models on OpenR1-50K for one epoch, following previous work ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . The models being trained receive Raw prompts without chat templates, matching the Base models’ text-completion format and keeping prompt formatting consistent across methods. Our Raw/Template baseline comparison supports this choice (Appendix B.1 ).

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate in-domain mathematical reasoning on AMC23 and AIME24 ( Li et al., 2024 ) , AIME25 and HMMT25 ( Balunović et al., 2025 ) , and Math500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) . OOD evaluations use HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , BBH ( Suzgun et al., 2023 ) , and NQ-Open ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) . For each group, we report mean accuracy, weighting the five in-domain or seven OOD datasets equally. Main results are averaged over two training seeds. Full training and evaluation settings, including original-model baselines, are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Learning and capability retention.
sections.text: As shown in Figure 1 (b), RLVR and Self-OPD (RLVR) combine mathematical gains with OOD accuracy close to Base. SFT and Self-OPD (SFT) generally incur larger OOD losses. Thus, Self-OPD with SFT and RLVR teachers shows different retention patterns even though both variants learn from student-generated responses. Limited SFT gains and modest forgetting in the smallest models are consistent with prior observations of difficulty learning long reasoning traces ( Li et al., 2025 ) and milder forgetting at smaller scales ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . OPD from larger Base teachers yields modest or inconsistent mathematical gains, accompanied by some OOD capability loss. OPSD largely preserves OOD accuracy, with details of its adaptation to Base models in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 4  Analysis
sections.text: We study the relationship between predictive distribution change and forgetting during post-training (Section 4.1 ). We then focus on OPD, examining how teacher information sources shape learning and retention (Section 4.2 ) and how students inherit teacher behavior through parameter and prediction trajectories (Section 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Teacher information and update selectivity.
sections.text: These OPD configurations produce markedly different retention and update selectivity. With the student initialization and distillation setup fixed, they differ in the additional information supplied by the teacher. We therefore examine what each teacher adds relative to student Base and how this information shapes update selectivity. We hypothesize that task-specific preferences concentrate updates in-domain, while general response habits also affect OOD predictions ( Wang et al., 2026 ) : • OPD from larger Base teachers. These teachers produce high student ρ \rho . Their feedback reflects cross-model pretraining differences spanning mathematics and many other tasks. Even when OPD trains only on mathematical problems, fitting these broader preferences may change OOD predictions through shared parameters, contributing to higher ρ \rho . • Self-OPD (SFT). Starting from the student’s Base, SFT fits the teacher’s predictions to fixed external reference answers through off-policy training, learning their solution content and response habits. Self-OPD then conveys these acquired preferences through the teacher’s token-level predictions on student-generated responses. The inherited response habits may also affect OOD behavior. • Self-OPD (RLVR). Starting from the student’s Base, RLVR adjusts the teacher’s distribution using correctness scores on its own on-policy responses. Self-OPD then conveys these reward-based adjustments through the teacher’s token-level predictions on student-generated responses. The acquired preference for higher-reward behavior may concentrate feedback more strongly on the target task. • OPSD. Teacher weights remain identical to student Base, while an in-domain mathematical reference solution supplies problem-specific evidence through context. This evidence may concentrate feedback on the current task. This hypothesis predicts that adding mathematical post-training to the same larger Base teacher will make its feedback more task-specific and lower student ρ \rho .

sections.heading: Self-OPD reproduces source-dependent learning and retention patterns.
sections.text: We pair each Self-OPD student with the SFT/RLVR run that produced its frozen teacher. Both start from the same Base; the source run provides a reference for the capabilities and behavior the student inherits. Students of RLVR teachers approach teacher task performance early with similar capability retention. Students of SFT teachers incur OOD declines approaching or exceeding their teachers’ (Appendix D.3 ). We examine whether these shared behavioral patterns correspond to similar parameter paths.

sections.heading: Models along parameter lines provide a capability reference.
sections.text: We characterize the learning and retention available along the parameter directions defined by these endpoints. We first interpolate and extrapolate the SFT, RLVR, and Self-OPD endpoints ( Huang et al., 2026 ) to examine changes in update magnitude: θ λ = θ 0 + λ ⁡ ( θ end − θ 0 ) . \theta_{\lambda}=\theta_{0}+\lambda(\theta_{\mathrm{end}}-\theta_{0}). The source SFT/RLVR endpoints are the frozen teachers, so their sweeps provide a capability reference along the Base–teacher line; Self-OPD sweeps examine the student’s own update direction. Student prefix and token probabilities weight teacher feedback; these weights and the logit Jacobians change along the student’s path (Appendix G.1 ). We first examine how readily students can generate their teachers’ response prefixes. On the same mathematical problems, SFT-teacher prefixes have lower probability under the shared Base than RLVR-teacher prefixes, and this difference persists during student training (Appendix D.4 ). Since OPD receives feedback on student-generated prefixes, teacher preferences associated with rarely visited prefixes have fewer opportunities to contribute to updates. This offers an explanation for slower transfer of SFT task gains relative to OOD changes. Response openings provide a concrete instance of this mismatch. In our diagnostics, SFT teachers inherit openings such as Okay and Alright from reference answers, while their preferred opening tokens fall outside the Base student’s Top-16 candidates. In Self-OPD (SFT), zeroing feedback at the first response position during training improves final mathematical accuracy by 3.36 percentage points on average across five models relative to ordinary feedback, while the OOD accuracy difference is at most 0.53 percentage points per model (Appendix D.5 ). This intervention shows that feedback tied to teacher response habits can impede task learning.

sections.heading: 5  Conclusion
sections.text: OPDArena provides a shared framework for comparing task learning, capability retention, and predictive distribution changes across SFT, RLVR, and OPD. Across these methods, OOD distribution change is more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain change, motivating ρ \rho as a measure of update selectivity. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that the preferences they acquire through in-domain post-training lead to more selective student updates. The student’s own distribution further shapes how these preferences are inherited. These findings motivate selecting OPD teachers by the information they add relative to student Base and its interaction with student predictions, alongside teacher capabilities.

sections.heading: Learning and forgetting in post-training.
sections.text: Acquiring new skills while retaining prior capabilities is a central problem in continual learning [ Wang et al., 2024 ] . Empirical studies show that language-model fine-tuning can impair capabilities beyond the target task, motivating evaluations that jointly measure adaptation and retention [ Luo et al., 2025 ] . For language-model post-training, prior work connects the retention advantage of online RL to limited KL changes on the new task [ Shenfeld et al., 2026 ] . A complementary study of multimodal language models analyzes how supervision distributions affect learning and interference with prior knowledge [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Our comparison examines this learning–forgetting relationship under token-level supervision from different teachers.

sections.heading: On-policy distillation.
sections.text: Training on student-generated trajectories exposes a distillation teacher to the contexts its student actually visits, reducing the mismatch between training and deployment distributions [ Agarwal et al., 2024 ] . MiniLLM uses reverse-KL distillation to align student and teacher predictions [ Gu et al., 2024 ] . Subsequent analysis identifies compatible thinking patterns and additional teacher capabilities as important conditions for successful OPD, and traces learning to alignment on high-probability tokens at student-visited states [ Li et al., 2026 ] . Related work also finds that smaller models can struggle to learn from strong reasoning demonstrations [ Li et al., 2025 ] . These studies motivate our analysis of how teacher preferences affect student predictions across domains.

sections.heading: Self-distillation and teacher information.
sections.text: Teacher information can enter through both model parameters and conditioning context. In OPSD, access to a reference solution provides the teacher with privileged information hidden from the student [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] . On-policy context distillation similarly transfers information available in a teacher’s context into student parameters [ Ye et al., 2026 ] . Teacher conditioning, update rules, and the response tokens receiving supervision influence the resulting training signal [ Zhao et al., 2026 , Ye et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2026 ] . On-policy delta distillation extracts post-training information through teacher log-probability differences [ Heo et al., 2026 ] . We use teacher comparisons and this decomposition to examine how contextual, pretrained, and post-trained preferences affect update selectivity.

sections.heading: Distribution changes and parameter paths.
sections.text: Prediction and parameter measurements provide complementary views of post-training. Distribution-based analyses connect supervision to changes in model behavior [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Complementary work jointly evaluates learning and retention across fine-tuning parameterizations and uses interpolation to study behavior along adaptation paths [ Huang et al., 2026 ] . We combine parameter and prediction measurements to examine how Self-OPD students acquire teacher behavior along their own training paths.

sections.heading: B.2  Training Input Formats
sections.text: All methods train on OpenR1-50K.

sections.heading: Rollout input format.
sections.text: All five Base models use Raw input for their rollout-based methods. The model receives only the original problem text: {ORIGINAL_PROBLEM} No system message, user/assistant delimiters, chat generation prefix, or empty thinking block is inserted. Student rollouts and in-domain validation use the same Raw protocol. For Self-OPD and OPD from larger models, teachers also use Raw input when scoring student-generated responses.

sections.heading: SFT input format.
sections.text: Raw SFT tokenizes the original problem as the prompt and its complete worked solution as the target, without chat-control tokens. An end-of-sequence token is appended to the solution. Cross-entropy loss is applied only to solution and end-of-sequence tokens; prompt tokens are masked. This convention applies to both Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 Base students.

sections.heading: OPSD teacher augmentation.
sections.text: The teacher receives the original problem with the following private block; the student receives only the original user content: Here is a privileged reference solution to the original problem: === Reference Solution Begin === {FULL_REFERENCE_SOLUTION} === Reference Solution End === Use the reference solution as private guidance. Independently solve the original problem, and produce the answer in the format requested in the original prompt. For the OPSD accuracy comparisons, we append Answer to the original problem: on a new line after the private block and before the student response. This preserves the explicit transition supplied by the original OPSD teacher’s chat prompt while using the Raw text-completion format of our Base models [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] . The student receives only the Raw problem, and the teacher scores its tokens. Appendix E compares three teacher input formats, their answer-boundary diagnostics, and full training results, and specifies the Raw-teacher configuration used for the distribution comparison.

sections.heading: In-domain.
sections.text: Raw tokenizes the dataset user content directly without chat control tokens. For example, the complete Raw input for the first AIME25 validation item is: Find the sum of all integer bases $b>9$ for which $17_{b}$ is a divisor of $97_{b}$. Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}. The in-domain evaluations along the training curves use this Raw format. Standalone baseline input modes are identified in the baseline tables.

sections.heading: OOD.
sections.text: All seven OOD tasks use task-native Raw input without a chat template. HellaSwag scores candidate endings appended to the activity and context. ARC-Challenge scores each answer after the question and choices. MMLU uses zero-shot subject prompts and scores answer letters. IFEval checks the official instruction constraints; TriviaQA uses flexible answer containment. BBH uses three chain-of-thought examples and exact-matches the extracted final answer, stopping at EOS or a newline followed by Q: ; paragraph breaks are allowed. We extract the last explicit conclusion, accepting capitalization, colon, “correct/final answer,” and boxed-answer variants. For multiple-choice tasks we retain the option label; for other tasks we extract the short answer in the required format, removing quotes and accompanying explanations. Otherwise, we use the text extracted after the first literal “the answer is” cue.

sections.heading: Appendix E OPSD: Teacher Input and Answer Boundaries
sections.text: OPSD uses privileged reference solutions to provide token-level feedback on student-generated answers. Its original implementation uses chat-formatted teacher prompts, which provide an explicit transition from reference material to the response being scored [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] . We adapt this transition to the Raw text-completion setting of our Base models and compare three ways of presenting the same reference information.

sections.heading: E.1  Three Teacher Input Formats
sections.text: In all three settings, the student receives the Raw problem and generates its own response. The teacher uses the same Base weights as the student’s initialization, receives the problem and full reference solution, and scores the student-generated tokens. The private reference block and instruction are given in Appendix B.2 . Only the teacher’s input formatting differs: • Raw: concatenate the problem, private reference block, and instruction as plain text, followed directly by the student response. • Chat template: package the same material as a user message and place the template’s assistant-start marker before the student response. • Raw + answer boundary: retain the Raw input and append Answer to the original problem: on a new line before the response. The resulting teacher prefixes have the following structure, where [private block] includes the reference and its instruction: Raw: [problem] [private block] [student response] Chat: <user> [problem] [private block] </user> <assistant> [student response] Boundary: [problem] [private block] Answer to the original problem: [student response] The role markers above are schematic; each model uses its corresponding template. Teacher weights remain those of the Base model in every setting. The original OPSD prompt likewise explicitly transitions from the reference solution to a new answer [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] .

These measurements suggest that simply removing the chat template can leave the Base teacher without a clear distinction between the completed reference solution and the student’s new answer. The assistant-start marker in the original prompting convention supplies this distinction; an explicit textual boundary preserves its role in a Raw prompt. Both forms of separation help the teacher provide feedback on the student’s own solution.

sections.text: The accuracy comparisons in Figure 1 (b) and Table 1 use a Raw student and a Raw teacher with the explicit answer boundary. The distribution comparison in Figure 3 retains the plain Raw/Raw control to match teacher and student formatting without additional answer-start cues. Both configurations provide the same privileged reference information to the teacher. The complete accuracy and JS comparisons here document the effects of this input adaptation.

sections.heading: Teacher input can affect update selectivity.
sections.text: Interestingly, Chat formatting consistently raises in-domain JS relative to Raw, while changes in OOD JS are much smaller in absolute size and its five-model mean remains nearly unchanged. Consequently, ρ \rho decreases. A textual answer boundary produces in-domain JS close to Chat formatting, showing that ordinary language cues can have a similar effect to role markers. These results suggest that teacher conditioning can introduce response preferences whose effects concentrate on the target domain. Together with the boundary variant’s accuracy improvements over plain Raw, they motivate optimizing teacher prompts to direct OPD feedback toward task learning while limiting accompanying OOD changes. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student’s pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain. Code: github.com/StellarCurtain/OPDArena 1 Introduction Post-training enables language models to acquire new skills, but can erode capabilities learned during pretraining ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Compared with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on fixed, off-policy responses, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often preserves prior capabilities better, a behavior linked to on-policy data and limited distributional change ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated responses with token-level teacher supervision ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . OPD shares the on-policy setting, yet retention outcomes vary substantially across teacher configurations ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . This raises the question of how OPD compares with SFT and RLVR in learning and capability retention, and how teacher choice shapes these outcomes. To answer the above question, we introduce OPDArena, a framework that systematically compares SFT, RLVR, and OPD across five Base models and four types of OPD teachers under a shared mathematical post-training setup. Figure 1 summarizes this comparison and reveals distinct learning and retention patterns: 1) RLVR and Self-OPD (RLVR) combine mathematical gains with strong retention, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) stays close to Base accuracy in both domains. 2) OPD from larger teachers and Self-OPD (SFT) incur more severe forgetting, while SFT has the largest average capability loss. To understand these differences, we examine changes in predictive distributions. Across methods, OOD change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. This motivates examining update selectivity, measured by OOD prediction change per unit of in-domain change, in relation to the information teachers provide relative to student Base. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that the preferences they acquire through SFT or RLVR concentrate student updates more strongly in-domain. The student’s own distribution further shapes how these preferences contribute to updates, helping explain the different rates at which task gains and forgetting are inherited. Our contributions are: • A systematic evaluation framework. OPDArena compares SFT, RLVR, and OPD teacher sources under a shared setup, jointly characterizing target-domain learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. • A refined view of distribution change and retention. We show that OOD distribution change is more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain change across student models and teacher configurations. We further use the OOD-to-in-domain change ratio, ρ \rho , to characterize update selectivity. • Teacher information and update selectivity. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that preferences acquired through SFT or RLVR improve student update selectivity. Further analyses identify mismatches between teacher-preferred responses and the student’s distribution that can hinder task learning, helping explain why task gains and forgetting transfer at different rates. RLVR and Self-OPD (RLVR) combine task learning with low forgetting. 2 Method We compare post-training methods applied to the same released Qwen Base models and measure their effects on mathematical learning and general capability retention. Across these methods, OOD distribution change is more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain change, motivating ρ \rho as a measure of update selectivity. Controlled comparisons of OPD teachers show that the preferences they acquire through in-domain post-training lead to more selective student updates. The student’s own distribution further shapes how these preferences are inherited. These findings motivate selecting OPD teachers by the information they add relative to student Base and its interaction with student predictions, alongside teacher capabilities. Appendix A Related Work Learning and forgetting in post-training. Acquiring new skills while retaining prior capabilities is a central problem in continual learning [ Wang et al., 2024 ] . Empirical studies show that language-model fine-tuning can impair capabilities beyond the target task, motivating evaluations that jointly measure adaptation and retention [ Luo et al., 2025 ] . For language-model post-training, prior work connects the retention advantage of online RL to limited KL changes on the new task [ Shenfeld et al., 2026 ] . A complementary study of multimodal language models analyzes how supervision distributions affect learning and interference with prior knowledge [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Our comparison examines this learning–forgetting relationship under token-level supervision from different teachers. On-policy distillation. Training on student-generated trajectories exposes a distillation teacher to the contexts its student actually visits, reducing the mismatch between training and deployment distributions [ Agarwal et al., 2024 ] . MiniLLM uses reverse-KL distillation to align student and teacher predictions [ Gu et al., 2024 ] . Subsequent analysis identifies compatible thinking patterns and additional teacher capabilities as important conditions for successful OPD, and traces learning to alignment on high-probability tokens at student-visited states [ Li et al., 2026 ] . Related work also finds that smaller models can struggle to learn from strong reasoning demonstrations [ Li et al., 2025 ] . These studies motivate our analysis of how teacher preferences affect student predictions across domains. Self-distillation and teacher information. Teacher information can enter through both model parameters and conditioning context. In OPSD, access to a reference solution provides the teacher with privileged information hidden from the student [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] . On-policy context distillation similarly transfers information available in a teacher’s context into student parameters [ Ye et al., 2026 ] . Teacher conditioning, update rules, and the response tokens receiving supervision influence the resulting training signal [ Zhao et al., 2026 , Ye et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2026 ] . On-policy delta distillation extracts post-training information through teacher log-probability differences [ Heo et al., 2026 ] . We use teacher comparisons and this decomposition to examine how contextual, pretrained, and post-trained preferences affect update selectivity. Distribution changes and parameter paths. Prediction and parameter measurements provide complementary views of post-training. Distribution-based analyses connect supervision to changes in model behavior [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Complementary work jointly evaluates learning and retention across fine-tuning parameterizations and uses interpolation to study behavior along adaptation paths [ Huang et al., 2026 ] . We combine parameter and prediction measurements to examine how Self-OPD students acquire teacher behavior along their own training paths.
